proposed_features.description: Identifies the main subject of the text, which strongly correlates with the domain (e.g., corporations vs. athletes vs. governments vs. researchers).
Describes the central event or state being reported, distinguishing between market movements, game outcomes, policy changes, and technical discoveries.
Indicates whether the text focuses on immediate results, long-term trends, or future projections, which varies by category (e.g., sports are immediate, business often trend-based).
Measures the frequency and type of numerical data (scores, financial figures, dates, technical specs) which helps distinguish data-heavy business/scitech from narrative-heavy world/sports.
Captures the tone and formality, ranging from objective reporting to sensationalized headlines or technical jargon.
Assesses the depth of cause-and-effect reasoning presented, distinguishing simple event reporting from complex geopolitical or market analysis.
Defines the breadth of impact, from individual/team level to global/macro-economic level, helping separate sports from world/business.
Identifies the primary verbs used, such as 'win/lose' (sports), 'approve/regulate' (world/scitech), or 'rise/fall' (business).
Measures the level of abstraction, from concrete physical events (sports) to abstract concepts (policy, market theory, code).
Detects language indicating immediacy or breaking news, common in sports and breaking world news, less so in long-form business analysis.
Assesses whether the text focuses on specific named entities (teams, companies, countries) or general categories (stocks, viruses, laws).
Describes the type of conflict or tension, such as competitive rivalry, legal dispute, political opposition, or technical vulnerability.
Indicates whether the outcome is definitive (final score, approved law) or probabilistic (market prediction, theoretical flaw).
Checks for specialized terminology unique to specific fields (e.g., 'PGA Tour', 'severance', 'antivirus engine', 'roadmap to democracy').
